DELIVERING ON COMPLEX BUILDING MAINTENANCE – THE ROLE AND IMPACT OF 
THE FACILITIES TEAM 
Galway County Council’s Facilities Team continues to demonstrate strong leadership and 
technical expertise in delivering complex building maintenance and conservation projects, 
as shown through recent works completed at: 
1. Maam Courthouse and  
2. Loughrea Library. 
These projects highlight both the Facilities team day to day operational capability as well as 
their strategic contribution to national policy objectives and the Council’s reputation for 
excellence. 
At Loughrea Library, the team addressed critical water ingress issues, protecting an essential 
public asset. The use of specialist contractors with rope access systems reflects a 
commitment to innovation, compliance, and best practice in health and safety, aligned with 
the Council’s ISO 45001 Health & Safety Management System. This demonstrates a culture 
where safety, quality, and service delivery are integrated. 
Furthermore, recent works at Maam Courthouse, a protected structure of significant 
cultural value to the County of Galway, further demonstrate our Facilities team’s expertise. 
Delivery required a coordinated, multi-disciplinary approach, including: 
• Navigating derogation licensing with the National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) 
due to a Horseshoe Bat roost 
• Engaging ecological consultants (MKO) to ensure compliance with environmental 
legislation 
• Securing Section 57 approval and working closely with our very experienced 
Conservation Officer 
• Coordinating with ESB Networks to safely de-energise the building 
• Preserving ecological pathways and addressing invasive species challenges 
This coordination reflects the complex regulatory environment in which local authorities 
operate, balancing heritage conservation, biodiversity protection, and infrastructure 
renewal. 
These projects support national and regional policy frameworks, including the National 
Planning Framework and Project Ireland 2040, where local authorities like Galway County 
Council play a key delivery role. The Facilities Team exemplifies this by delivering place-
based outcomes that enhance community assets while safeguarding environmental and 
cultural heritage.

8 
 
Furthermore, the successful delivery of such projects reinforces Galway County Council’s 
position as a high-performing, solution-focused local authority, demonstrating 
professionalism, innovation, and accountability. 
Our Facilities Team are: 
• Protecting and enhancing heritage assets as well as critical infrastructure assets 
• Demonstrating leadership in compliance and environmental stewardship 
• Supporting the delivery of national strategic objectives at a local level 
• Reinforcing Galway County Councils' reputation for excellence 
Their work is central to ensuring the continued provision of safe, sustainable, and high-
quality facilities for communities now and into the future, within the full expanse of the 
county.

OUR LEISURE CENTRES –  POWERING A GREENER FUTURE 
 
We are delighted to announce the completion of the new Solar PV array installation to the 
Ballinasloe Leisure centre. This project was initiated approximately 12months ago in 
partnership between the Corporate Services Facilities team, Coral Leisure Ltd and Exemplar 
Energy.  The project underwent rigorous planning,  design and procurement process to

of our community leisure spaces.  
The new rooftop system in Ballinasloe will generate approximately 100,000 kWh of clean, 
renewable electricity every year, helping to reduce reliance on grid electricity and lower the 
carbon footprint for the Leisure Centre.

RECREATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 
The Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht, Dara Calleary TD, 
has announced the launch of the 2026–2027 Outdoor Recreation Infrastructure Scheme 
(ORIS), which supports the development and enhancement of outdoor recreational

15 
 
infrastructure in rural areas. Galway County Council, working with local communities and 
stakeholders, will progress applications under the scheme. 
ORIS provides funding across three measures: 
• Measure 1: up to €40,000 for small-scale repair, maintenance, and promotion 
• Measure 2: up to €200,000 for medium-scale upgrades and new amenity 
development 
• Measure 3: up to €500,000 for large-scale and strategic projects 
A Project Development Measure (PDM) also supports the advancement of “shovel-ready” 
projects, allowing up to four applications (max €100,000 combined), with additional 
provision for equestrian trails and Gaeltacht/offshore island projects (up to €50,000 each). 
All projects must meet scheme requirements, including planning, environmental screening, 
and landowner consent. Key deadlines are expected in August and November 2026, with 
application forms to issue shortly on Galway.ie. 
ORIS continues to support a range of projects across Galway, including upgrades to the 
Western Way, improvements along the Kylemore Road–Hymany Way, works at Glinsk 
Heritage Park, project development in Portumna, and Rinville walkway extensions.

UNESCO GALWAY CITY OF FILM – SHORT DOCUMENTARY BURSARY 2026  
The Galway County recipient of the Short Documentary Bursary 2026 is Turloughmore based 
filmmaker Jamie Costello.  
Across his work, Jamie plays with the documentary form blending it with unconventional 
fiction-based worlds to create films that are captivating, immersive and honest. 
Through this bursary Jamie will create ‘Getting Lost in the Garden’. The sudden death of a 
family dog forces a mother and father to confront time, loss and the quiet approach of their 
own mortality. Getting Lost in the Garden is a poetic documentary centered around the 
unexpected death of a family dog and the quiet unfulfilled void it leaves behind. Led by the 
personal recollections of a mother and father, the film sits in the liminal moments of 
passing. 
“I am delighted to have received this bursary as it gives me purpose as a filmmaker and a 
sense of belonging. Even though this is only the beginning. The Ardán Short Documentary 
Bursary marks my starting point as a professional director and feeds the motivation to push 
myself to reach the next step in my career.” - Jamie Costello

Baile Chláir Guided Biodiversity Walk to Celebrate Exciting New Public Art Sculpture! 
• Biodiversity Walk with artist Cathal McCarthy 
• Saturday 13 June, 12 noon - 1.30pm 
• Starting at the Roots Café, Baile Chláir Village 
• Free and open to all.  
Herbalist Sharon Walsh and Artist Cathal McCarthy 
embarked on a special guided biodiversity walk on Saturday 
13 June at 12 noon, in Baile Chláir.  
The walk will explore the flora, fauna and native plant life 
that are inspiring the sculpture Unfurl a new sculpture that 
has been commissioned for Baile Chláir. The artwork will 
feature stainless steel ribbons of text which will reflect the 
rich heritage of Baile Chláir and also inspiration from the 
local community, history and archaeology. It will include 
some new lyrics created by students from Coláiste Bhaile 
Chláir via song writing workshops with The Saw Doctors’ 
Leo Moran and songwriter Padraig Stevens. 
The walk will trace the route of the Clare river, roadside verges, fields and surroundings of 
the village. Your guide Sharon Walsh will highlight the grasses, wildflowers and hedgerow 
species that are native to the locale.  
Participants will learn how to use herbs for tea making and how biodiversity is being 
celebrated in the creation of this new permanent cultural landmark. Following the walk, the 
group will return to the SMA centre for herbal tea and a short presentation on the 
development of the sculpture by visual artist Cathal McCarthy  
The Unfurl sculpture aims to address unique heritage of Baile Chláir, the castle and friary 
ruins, the Nine Arch Bridge, place-names, and the musical spirit of the song The N17 itself. 
"The sculpture aims to be like a new song for Baile Chláir, created with input from local 
groups via arts participation and engagement " McCarthy said. "The Biodiversity walk is a

chance to see the vibrant and indigenous plants and 
places that will live on in the work for the future”. 
The new sculpture by Artist Cathal McCarthy is a 
Galway County Arts Office and OPW Commission 
funded by the Per Cent for Art programme with 
contributions from students of Coláiste Bhaile Chláir 
and local community groups and managed by Rina 
Whyte, Public Art Curator. 
 
CREATIVE PLACES TUAM BEGINS NEW CHAPTER UNDER LOCAL LEADERSHIP WITH 
ARTS COUNCIL AWARD 
 
Creative Places Tuam has secured Arts Council funding for 2026 and 2027, paving the way 
for a new phase of the community-led arts programme under local leadership. 
 
The initiative, which supports artists, funds community projects and promotes cultural 
activity in Tuam and surrounding areas, will become fully locally based from 2027. 
Governance will transfer from Create, the national agency for collaborative arts, to Galway 
County Council's Arts Office.  
Residents, artists, community groups and organisations are invited to take part in the next 
phase of the programme. The programme for 2026 and 2027 has been shaped by 
consultation with Tuam’s creative community and feedback gathered through an artist 
survey in 2025.  
New initiatives will include monthly one-to-one mentoring sessions known as Soundboard 
121, the Graft Series for networking and knowledge exchange, and Loop Sessions, informal 
creative meet-ups. The programme will also include 
screenings, an Open Call, Art cArt outings, Sounding Tuam, 
three artist residencies and the Cultural Growth Fund, 
which organisers say has seen a 40% increase in

CRUINNIÚ AR NA HOILEÁIN 
For the third year in a row, we were successful in securing additional funding to run a full 
programme as Gaeilge across all three Aran Islands. This amount came to €10,000. The 
additional costs and challenges with programming for the islands meant that every last 
penny of this was needed. As well as bringing facilitators from the mainland, we were also 
able to fund at least one artist from each island to carry out 
creative workshops, thereby contributing to the economic 
development of the islands. Our staff were out on the islands 
on the day and saw firsthand how much of an impact the 
programme has. There was puppetry, drama, music, 
spraypainting, circus skills, and even a silent disco! 
The kids begged us to please come back next year, and one 
child said as he was taking his new puppet home, “I never 
knew that I could make something like this”. That sums up 
what Cruinniú na nÓg is all about.

THE WATERSPORTS INCLUSION GAMES 2026  
Galway Sports Partnership are delighted to 
support The Watersports Inclusion Games 2026 
which were officially launched at Galway Hooker 
Sailing Club on 8th June 2026, with the event 
scheduled for 11–12 July in the Port of Galway. 
This free national event promotes inclusive 
participation in watersports for people of all 
abilities, ages, and backgrounds. First established in 2017, the Games will feature activities 
such as sailing, kayaking, canoeing, water skiing, and sensory experiences, with an 
anticipated 400 participants and 300 volunteers taking part across the weekend. 
Led by Irish Sailing Association, in partnership with National Governing Bodies of Sport such 
as Dive Ireland, Canoeing Ireland and several local clubs and organisations, the Games aim 
to increase accessibility and inclusion in watersports nationwide. Supported by Sport Ireland 
funding and a wide network of partners, the event also highlights ongoing efforts to align 
with national inclusion policies. With strong community involvement and leadership, 
including Ambassador Mark Henderson, the Games continue to serve as a key fixture in the 
summer watersports calendar, promoting active participation and inclusive opportunities 
for all. 
The Games are due to take place on the weekend of the 11 – 12 July. For further details and

Galway Public Libraries is set to deliver a first for Ireland with the introduction of the 
country’s first modern mobile library vehicles based on bus infrastructure, following the 
signing of contracts by Galway County Council for the design and construction of two new 
state-of-the-art units. 
The contracts have been awarded to Spanish specialist manufacturer Alegria-Activity, 
marking the company’s first project in Ireland. Funding for the initiative is being provided by 
Galway County Council, with support from the Department of Rural and Community 
Development and the Gaeltacht under the Library Capital Programme. 
The vehicles will significantly modernise and expand the Galway Mobile Library Service, 
enabling books, learning resources and wider community supports to be delivered to towns, 
villages, schools and rural communities across the county. The new generation units will 
function as fully equipped mobile service points, with shelving, staff workspace, enhanced IT 
capacity and provision for public printing, supported by onboard power and connectivity 
systems. 
Cathaoirleach of the County of Galway Cllr David Collins welcomed the investment, saying it 
represents “a strong statement of the Council’s commitment to vibrant communities and 
equal access to library services, regardless of location.” 
Chief Executive of Galway County Council, Liam Conneally, said the investment “reflects our 
commitment to inclusion, accessibility and sustainable community development. These new 
vehicles will strengthen and future-proof the Mobile Library Service, ensuring communities 
across Galway continue to have access to high-quality library services.” 
Liz Keane, Galway City & County Librarian, said the project represents “a significant 
investment in the future of our Mobile Library Service,” adding that the partnership

54 
 
combines local experience with international expertise to deliver “modern, flexible vehicles 
that will serve communities across Galway for many years to come.” 
“The investment underlines its ongoing commitment to innovation, accessibility and 
delivering high-quality library services to communities throughout the county,” she added. 
Operating since 1960, the Mobile Library Service has long played a key role in connecting 
communities with reading, learning and cultural opportunities. 
Designed in collaboration with Alegria-Activity, the new vehicles will feature modern 
technology, improved accessibility and flexible layouts to meet the evolving needs of library 
users across the county.

HOUSING ALLOCATIONS REPORT 2025 – STATUTORY RETURN UNDER SECTION 
22(12), HOUSING (MISCELLANEOUS PROVISIONS) ACT 2009 
As Chief Executive, I wish to acknowledge that Galway County Council continues to face 
significant housing challenges, characterised by sustained demand, ongoing pressures 
within homelessness services, and constraints within the housing supply system. The 
increase in households presenting to emergency accommodation reflects broader national 
trends and reinforces the need for a continued, proactive response focused on prevention, 
timely allocation, and accelerating exits into secure tenancies.

68 
 
Notwithstanding these challenges, there are strong grounds for confidence. Galway County 
Council is supported by an active development pipeline and a high level of engagement 
across the Council, Approved Housing Bodies, and delivery partners. While infrastructure 
and system constraints can affect the pace of delivery, there is a shared commitment to 
improving coordination and bringing forward housing schemes at greater scale and speed. 
This report is prepared in accordance with Section 22(12) of the Housing (Miscellaneous 
Provisions) Act 2009, which requires the Chief Executive to submit to the Elected Members 
an annual statement of allocations made under the Council’s Allocation Scheme, specifying 
the categories of dwellings and households and the proportion of each category. It provides 
a detailed account of allocations completed during 2025 and situates this activity within the 
broader context of housing demand, supply constraints, and ongoing delivery across County 
Galway. 
Housing delivery remains a central priority for the Council, with a robust programme of new 
build, acquisition, and partnership delivery underway across social, affordable, and cost 
rental housing. This approach is ensuring a steady flow of new homes, while also targeting 
supports towards those in greatest need, including households experiencing homelessness 
and those with medical or disability related requirements. The progress made to date, 
together with the strength of the current pipeline, provides a positive foundation for 
continued delivery and improved outcomes for households across County Galway. 
SOCIAL HOUSING ALLOCATIONS TO LA AND AHB HOUSING PROPERTIES 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
A total of 286 allocations were completed across the administrative area during 2025. When 
analysed by bedroom requirement, the profile of allocations aligns closely with demand, 
with a strong concentration in 2- and 3-bedroom accommodation, while continuing to meet 
a consistent level of need for 1-bedroom units. It is important to note that 2-bedroom 
allocations (108 units) are drawn from both the 1 and 2-bedroom waiting lists and therefore 
form part of the Council’s response to combined smaller household demand.

69 
 
In overall terms, 1- and 2-bedroom allocations total 158 units (50 one bed and 108 two 
bed), representing the largest share of delivery and supporting single applicants, couples, 
and smaller households, including those exiting homelessness or supported 
accommodation. Three-bedroom homes accounted for 99 allocations, continuing to 
represent the core provision for family households. Larger family accommodation 
comprised a smaller but important element of delivery, including 21 four-bedroom homes, 
together with 8 allocations across five- and six-bedroom units, reflecting both the limited 
availability of such stock and the targeted allocation of larger homes. 
The underlying basis of need remains consistent across all bedroom categories, with 
allocations predominantly driven by acute housing pressures. In particular, 100 households 
were previously supported through rent supplement/HAP, while 66 households were 
accommodated from homeless services, institutions, emergency accommodation or hostels, 
demonstrating the continued prioritisation of exits from homelessness across all unit sizes. 
From a medical and vulnerability perspective, housing need arising from disability continues 
to feature strongly, including 24 allocations on mental health grounds and 22 on physical 
disability grounds, alongside allocations relating to intellectual, sensory, and unspecified 
disability. There were also 14 households accommodated due to involuntary sharing, and a 
further 14 cases where mortgages were deemed unsustainable, requiring social housing 
intervention. Additional allocations arose from unfit accommodation (11 cases), as well as 
overcrowding, exceptional medical or compassionate grounds, financial hardship, and 
unsuitable household circumstances. 
At smaller household level, the combined 1- and 2-bedroom provision (158 units) 
demonstrates a flexible response to need, with 2-bedroom homes also supporting 
households qualified for 1 bedroom accommodation where appropriate. The 3-bedroom 
category (99 units) remains essential to meeting the needs of families with children and 
those experiencing overcrowding or unsuitable living conditions, while larger units continue 
to be allocated on a targeted basis to address specific family requirements.

70 
 
SOCIAL HOUSING DEMAND 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The current social housing demand profile highlights a significant and sustained level of 
need across the county, with a total of 2,964 approved households awaiting 
accommodation. When analysed in line with standard reporting practice, combined demand 
for 1- and 2-bedroom accommodation is notably high at 1,719 households, reflecting a 
substantial requirement from single person households, older persons, and smaller 
household types. Demand for family accommodation also remains strong, with 1,054 
households requiring 3-bedroom homes, while need for larger properties is more limited in 
volume, comprising 191 households across 4 bedroom and larger categories. 
Geographically, demand is most concentrated in key growth areas, including Athenry and 
Environs (484 households) and Oranmore/Baile Chláir (439 households), followed by Tuam 
(354 households) and Loughrea and Environs (246 households). However, there is also a 
consistent spread of demand across Ballinasloe, Connemara, and rural districts, 
demonstrating that housing need is both significant and county wide. Overall, the demand 
profile equates to approximately 58% for 1- and 2-bedroom need, 36% for 3-bedroom need, 
and 6% for 4 bedroom and larger households, reinforcing the requirement for a delivery 
programme that prioritises smaller units while maintaining a strong and consistent supply of 
family sized homes. 
Galway County Council currently manages an LA housing stock of 3,121 units, of which 3,036 
are occupied and 85 are vacant, resulting in an overall vacancy rate of 2.72%, marginally 
above the national benchmark of 2%. This variance equates to approximately 23 units and is

71 
 
influenced by a combination of operational and structural factors rather than day to day 
void management performance. 
In operational terms, performance remains strong. The Council is currently achieving the 
national void turnaround target of 18 weeks, with standard reletting activity (including units 
requiring minor works) averaging 17.27 weeks. A proportion of vacant units are at various 
stages of re letting, including 20 units available for allocation and 29 units undergoing minor 
repairs. 
The primary impact on vacancy levels arises from a relatively small number of complex 
cases. This includes 6 units requiring major refurbishment, most of which involve 
exceptional circumstances such as fire damage, storm damage, or legal issues, and 30 units 
classified as derelict. These derelict properties are not part of the active letting stock and 
are progressing through longer term programmes, including sale and regeneration, but 
nonetheless have a disproportionate impact on headline vacancy figures.  When completed, 
the average turnaround target will result in this council exceeding the National target. 
When these structurally constrained units are excluded, the Council’s effective vacancy rate 
reduces to 1.76%, which is below the national target. This confirms that, from an 
operational perspective, the Council is performing in line with national expectations, with 
the reported variance attributable primarily to legacy housing stock requiring 
redevelopment or disposal rather than delays in standard re letting activity. 
Overall, the position demonstrates that housing stock is being actively managed, with strong 
turnaround performance and a clear programme in place to address more complex vacant 
units through regeneration and other structural interventions. 
CONCLUSION 
In conclusion, Galway County Council continues to operate within a challenging housing 
environment characterised by sustained demand, pressures within homelessness services, 
and constraints in supply. Notwithstanding these pressures, the data demonstrates a clear 
and structured response by the Council, with 286 allocations delivered in 2025, targeted 
towards those in greatest need, including households exiting homelessness and those with 
medical or social vulnerabilities. 
The allocation profile reflects a balanced and needs based approach, with a strong focus on 
1- and 2-bedroom provision (158 allocations) to address smaller household demand, 
alongside consistent allocation of 3-bedroom homes (99 allocations) to support family 
housing needs. This aligns closely with the current demand profile, where the majority of 
households require smaller units, while maintaining the capacity to respond to larger family 
requirements where necessary. 
Demand remains significant, with 2,964 households on the waiting list, and a clear 
concentration of need in both smaller household accommodation and family housing across 
all areas of the county. At the same time, the Council’s housing stock is being actively

72 
 
managed, with void turnaround performance meeting national targets and an effective 
vacancy rate below the benchmark when structurally constrained units are excluded. This 
evidences strong operational performance, notwithstanding the impact of legacy derelict 
stock on headline figures. 
Overall, the position reflects a housing system that is functioning effectively within existing 
constraints, supported by an active delivery pipeline and ongoing investment. The 
combination of targeted allocations, strong stock management, and continued expansion of 
supply provides a solid foundation to improve outcomes, sustain exits from homelessness, 
and respond to the evolving housing needs of communities across County Galway.

Zero Emissions Vehicles Ireland (ZEVI) was set up in 2022 to develop and roll out Electric 
Vehicle Charging Infrastructure across Ireland.  This will include installation of new public EV 
charging hubs and the upgrading of existing EV charger locations.  ZEVI is currently part of 
the Department of Transport and is now being managed under the umbrella of Transport 
Infrastructure Ireland (TII). 
A National Audit of Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure across all Local Authorities areas 
has now actively started.  Each EV Charging Hub/Station in County Galway is being verified 
on site by LA personnel, photographed and technical details (such as power output, 
connector type) are being recorded.  A Mobile Phone App has been developed by ZEVI to 
enable Local Authorities to capture this data real-time during a site visit following which the 
data is then uploaded to a TII Asset Management System (AMS). It is intended that this data 
collection/audit will be completed mid Jul 2026.  This data repository, and its subsequent

COASTWATCH SEAGRASS CITIZEN SCIENCE WORKSHOP (KINVARA) 
The Biodiversity Office supported a Coastwatch-led seagrass citizen science workshop in 
Kinvara, focused on coastal biodiversity recording and monitoring. 30 participants from 
across Ireland attended and included scientists, NPWS staff, third level students, community 
group members and local authority staff.  Seagrass beds along the Galway coastline remain 
under-recorded, and this workshop aimed to address this gap by training participants in 
survey and recording techniques. 
Speakers at the event included Karin Dubsky from Coastwatch, Rosina Joyce, ecologist Cilian 
Roden and Juan Lugilde Yáñez from the University of Galway. The event highlighted the 
ecological importance of seagrass habitats for biodiversity, water quality and climate 
resilience, while actively contributing to increased data collection. The outputs from this 
workshop will support the mapping of seagrass beds around Ireland and help inform future 
measures to protect and

LOCAL BIODIVERSITY ACTION FUND (LBAF) 2026 
The National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS), through the Department of Housing, Local 
Government and Heritage, has announced the 2026 Local Biodiversity Action Fund (LBAF), 
with Galway County Council awarded €96,700 to deliver a range of biodiversity projects 
across the county. 
The LBAF is a key national funding stream supporting local authorities in implementing 
actions under the National Biodiversity Action Plan. It focuses on biodiversity conservation, 
restoration, monitoring and community engagement, with a strong emphasis on generating 
high-quality data and measurable outcomes to inform national biodiversity policy and 
management. 
The 2026 programme includes the following projects: 
MONITORING AND REMOVAL OF ALPINE NEWT 
Continued targeted work to control and remove populations of Alpine Newt, an invasive 
species which poses a significant threat to native amphibians. This project builds on

128 
 
previous years’ work and is considered a priority for preventing further spread and 
progressing towards eradication. 
GALWAY RAISED BOGS BIRD BASELINE SURVEY 
A survey of bird populations associated with raised bog habitats to establish baseline 
ecological data. This will support peatland restoration initiatives and address a recognised 
knowledge gap in understanding bird species’ dependence on these habitats. 
COUNTY GALWAY WETLANDS SURVEY (2026–2028) 
A major multi-annual project to collate, map and analyse wetland habitats across the 
county. The project will develop a comprehensive database and GIS layer of wetland sites, 
strengthening the evidence base for planning, conservation and future monitoring and 
supporting identification of priority areas for protection and restoration. 
WEST CONNACHT ISLANDS INVASIVE SPECIES MANAGEMENT PROGRAMME 
A programme of survey and control measures targeting invasive species on offshore islands. 
The project aims to protect sensitive island habitats and prevent further spread of invasive 
species that threaten native biodiversity. 
PRELIMINARY LAGOON SURVEY – CAMUS BAY, CONNEMARA 
A targeted survey of lagoon habitat, which is currently in unfavourable conservation status 
nationally. The project will provide valuable new data on this under-recorded habitat type 
and support future conservation and management measures. 
SURVEY OF INVASIVE AQUATIC SPECIES (DIKEROGAMMARUS HAEMOBAPHES) 
A focused survey to determine the distribution of this invasive aquatic species, supporting 
early detection and informing management responses at both local and national level. 
Delivery of these projects will involve collaboration with a range of partners including 
research institutions, NGOs and local stakeholders, and will contribute to strengthening the 
evidence base, informing conservation action and supporting biodiversity policy 
implementation at county level.
